name: OCSF System Activity
description: OCSF 1.9.0 System Activity event classes (snapshot from schema.ocsf.io).

fields.description: The normalized identifier of the process injection method.
The process injection method, normalized to the caption of the injection_type_id value. In the case of 'Other', it is defined by the event source.

A human-readable description providing additional context about the event outcome. Use this to convey details that go beyond the normalized status_id and source-specific status_code , such as a failure reason or error message. For example: "Account locked after 5 failed attempts." .

The primary timestamp of the event - when the activity actually occurred at the source. This does not capture when the event record was created or serialized by the source system; for event lifecycle timestamps such as ingestion and processing, use metadata.logged_time and metadata.processed_time respectively, or the equivalent attributes in the metadata.loggers array when recording pipeline stage

The time of the earliest event in an aggregate ( count > 1). Do not populate for discrete, point-in-time events - use time alone. Subclasses such as findings may redefine this for their own time-range semantics.

The full name of the observable attribute. The name is a pointer/reference to an attribute within the OCSF event data. For example: file.name . Array attributes may be represented in one of three ways. For example: resources.uid , resources[].uid , resources[0].uid .
The observable value type name.

The value associated with the observable attribute. The meaning of the value depends on the observable type. If the name refers to a scalar attribute, then the value is the value of the attribute. If the name refers to an object attribute, then the value is not populated.

The OCSF event type UID ( type_uid ) of the source event that this observable was extracted from. This field enables filtering and categorizing observables by their originating event type. For example: 300101 for Network Activity (class_uid 3001) with activity_id 1.
The observable value type identifier.

The unique identifier ( metadata.uid ) of the source OCSF event from which this observable was extracted. This field enables linking observables back to their originating event data when observables are stored in a separate location or system.
Contains the original and normalized reputation scores.

The unique identifier of a class. A class describes the attributes available in an event. Producers and mappers must set this to the uid defined in the event class definition. For example, Detection Finding is 2004 .

The time of the most recent event in an aggregate ( count > 1). Do not populate for discrete, point-in-time events - use time alone. Subclasses such as findings may redefine this for their own time-range semantics.
The version of the API service.
Details pertaining to the API request.
The information pertaining to the API service.
The information pertaining to the API group.
Details pertaining to the API response.
Verb/Operation associated with the request

The API or client token used to authenticate or authorize the API request. This attribute contains the base token object that represents: (1) IdP-issued client tokens (type_id: 6) such as Okta API tokens or Microsoft Entra ID Application Registration client secrets, or (2) generic API tokens/keys (type_id: 7) used for SaaS application authentication. Use this attribute when the API request was aut
The permissions that were granted to the process in a platform-native format.
The risk level, normalized to the caption of the risk_level_id value.
The normalized identifier for the specific type of Launch activity.
The malware name, as reported by the detection engine.
A unique identifier for the specific malware instance, as assigned by the detection engine (e.g., virus signature ID or IPS rule ID).
The list of file objects representing files that were identified as infected by the malware.
The severity of the malware, normalized to the captions of the severity_id values. In the case of 'Other', they are defined by the event source.
The list of normalized identifiers of the malware classifications.
The list of malware classifications, normalized to the captions of the classification_ids values. In the case of 'Other', they are defined by the event source.
The list of Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) identifiers associated with the malware.
The number of files that were identified to be infected by the malware.
The name or identifier of the security solution or service that provided the malware detection information.
The normalized identifier of the malware severity.
The uid attribute in numeric form where applicable. Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.
The module type.
The module file object.
The memory address where the module was loaded.
Details about the invocation of the function given in function_name .

The invoked function in the module. For load and unload events, this is the entry-point function of the module. The system calls the entry-point function whenever a process or thread loads or unloads the module.
The load type, normalized to the caption of the load_type_id value. In the case of 'Other', it is defined by the event source.
The normalized identifier for how the module was loaded in memory.
The start address of the execution.
Additional data about the policy such as the underlying JSON policy itself or other details.
The policy name. For example: AdministratorAccess Policy .
The policy type. For example: Identity Policy, Resource Policy, Service Control Policy, etc. .
The policy version number.
The policy group.
The description of the policy.
A unique identifier of the policy instance.
A determination if the content of a policy was applied to a target or request, or not.
The uid attribute in numeric form where applicable. Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.
The enrichment data associated with the attribute and value. The meaning of this data depends on the type the enrichment record.
The name of the attribute to which the enriched data pertains.
The enrichment type. For example: location .
The value of the attribute to which the enriched data pertains.
A long description of the enrichment data.
The time when the enrichment data was generated.
The enrichment data provider name.
The reputation of the enrichment data.
A short description of the enrichment data.
The URL of the source of the enrichment data.
The time when the enrichment data was generated.

The primary timestamp of the event - when the activity actually occurred at the source. This does not capture when the event record was created or serialized by the source system; for event lifecycle timestamps such as ingestion and processing, use metadata.logged_time and metadata.processed_time respectively, or the equivalent attributes in the metadata.loggers array when recording pipeline stage
The confidence score as reported by the event source. If confidence_id is 99 'Other', it should be the same as confidence if both are populated.
The time when the event was transmitted from the logging device to it's next destination.
The original size of the OCSF event data in kilobytes before any truncation occurred. This field is typically populated when is_truncated is true to indicate the full size of the original event.
The log system or component where the data originated. For example, a file path, syslog server name or a Windows hostname and logging subsystem such as Security.
The time when the event was last modified or enriched.
The list of labels attached to the event. For example: ["sample", "dev"]
The level at which an event was logged. This can be log provider specific. For example the audit level.
The unique tenant identifier.
The schema extensions used to create the event.

The source of the event or finding. This can be any distinguishing name for the logical origin of the data — for example, 'CloudTrail Events', or a use case like 'Attack Simulations' or 'Vulnerability Scans'.
The type of the event or finding as a subset of the source of the event. This can be any distinguishing characteristic of the data. For example 'Management Events' or 'Device Penetration Test'.
The list of profiles used to create the event. Profiles should be referenced by their name attribute for core profiles, or extension/name for profiles from extensions.

The ultimate logged time in the event pipeline - when the event reached its final destination (e.g., SIEM, data lake). If loggers is populated, this should match the logged_time of the last entry in the loggers array. This is distinct from time (when the activity occurred) and processed_time (when an intermediate system processed the event).
The event log name, typically for the consumer of the event. For example, the storage bucket name, SIEM repository index name, etc.
Sequence number of the event. The sequence number is a value available in some events, to make the exact ordering of events unambiguous, regardless of the event time precision.

An ordered array of Logger objects describing each hop in the event pipeline between the source and its final destination. Each entry captures the logging product, device, and timestamps ( logged_time , transmit_time ) at that stage. The last entry's logged_time should match metadata.logged_time .
The identifier of the original event. For example the numerical Windows Event Code or Cisco syslog code.
The entity from which the event or finding was first reported.

The time when the event was processed by an intermediate system (e.g., ETL pipeline, event processor) before reaching its final destination. Can be used with logged_time to calculate queuing duration via total_queued_duration .
The product that reported the event.

A unique identifier used to correlate this OCSF event with other related OCSF events, distinct from the event's uid value. This enables linking multiple OCSF events that are part of the same activity, transaction, or security incident across different systems or time periods.

The ultimate logged time in the event pipeline - when the event reached its final destination (e.g., SIEM, data lake). If loggers is populated, this should match the logged_time of the last entry in the loggers array. This is distinct from time (when the activity occurred) and processed_time (when an intermediate system processed the event).
The list of tags; {key:value} pairs associated to the event.
The format of data in the log where the data originated. For example CSV, XML, Windows Multiline, JSON, syslog or Cisco Log Schema.
A list of Data Classification objects, that include information about data classification levels and data category types, identified by a classifier.
The version of the OCSF schema, using Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer). For example: 1.0.0 . Event consumers use the version to determine the available event attributes.
The logging provider or logging service that logged the event. For example AWS CloudWatch or Splunk.

The amount of time an event spent in a queue awaiting processing. In this case, the value is the difference between processed_time and logged_time . This duration is inclusive of all queues between the originator of the event and the intended long-term storage destination of the event.
Debug information about non-fatal issues with this OCSF event. Each issue is a line in this string array.

The original event time as reported by the event source, preserved as a pass-through string in its native format (e.g., Syslog timestamp, Windows event time). This is not normalized to timestamp_t - the normalized equivalent is the base event time attribute. Omit if the event is generated rather than collected via logs.

The unique identifier assigned to the event in its original logging system before transformation to OCSF format. This field preserves the source system's native event identifier, enabling traceability back to the raw log entry. For example, a Windows Event Record ID, a syslog message ID, a Splunk _cd value, or a database transaction log sequence number.

The time when the event was processed by an intermediate system (e.g., ETL pipeline, event processor) before reaching its final destination. Can be used with logged_time to calculate queuing duration via total_queued_duration .
A unique identifier assigned to the OCSF event. This ID is specific to the OCSF event itself and is distinct from the original event identifier in the source system (see original_event_uid ).
The time when the event was last modified or enriched.
The time when the event was transmitted from the logging device to it's next destination.
The event log schema version of the original event. For example the syslog version or the Cisco Log Schema version
An array of transformation info that describes the mappings or transforms applied to the data.
Indicates whether the OCSF event data has been truncated due to size limitations. When true , some event data may have been omitted to fit within system constraints.

The original event/finding data as received from the source, before normalization into OCSF. Populate this with the verbatim log line, JSON payload, or other native format for forensic and debugging purposes. This field is not intended for structured querying - use the normalized OCSF attributes instead.
The administrator-supplied or application-generated name of the scan. For example: "Home office weekly user database scan", "Scan folders for viruses", "Full system virus scan"
The total size in bytes of all files that were scanned.
The type of scan.
The application-defined unique identifier assigned to an instance of a scan.
The timestamp indicating when the scan job began execution.
The type id of the scan.
The timestamp indicating when the scan job completed execution.
The timestamp indicating when the scan job began execution.
The timestamp indicating when the scan job completed execution.
The total number of files analyzed during the scan.
The total number of files identified as infected with malware during the scan.
The total number of storage volumes examined during the malware scan.
The uid attribute in numeric form where applicable. Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.
The number of unique malware detected across all infected files.

A container for source-specific attributes that do not map to any defined OCSF attribute. Use this to preserve valuable source data that would otherwise be lost during normalization. The keys and values are specific to the event source. Note: Consumers should not rely on a stable structure within this field. The preferred approach to unmapped attributes is to create a custom extension with the des
Indicates whether the device has an active mobile account. For example, this is indicated by the itunesStoreAccountActive value within JAMF Pro mobile devices.
The time when the device was last known to have been modified.
The endpoint operating system.
The International Mobile Equipment Identity values that are associated with the device.
The event occurred on a compliant device.
The network zone or LAN segment.
The image used as a template to run the virtual machine.
The identity of the service or user account that owns the endpoint or was last logged into it.
The event occurred on a shared device.
The time the system was booted.
The risk level, normalized to the caption of the risk_level_id value.

The event occurred on a supervised device. Devices that are supervised are typically mobile devices managed by a Mobile Device Management solution and are restricted from specific behaviors such as Apple AirDrop.
The device type. For example: unknown , server , desktop , laptop , tablet , mobile , virtual , browser , or other .
The group names to which the device belongs. For example: ["Windows Laptops", "Engineering"] .
The initial discovery time of the device.
The network domain where the device resides. For example: work.example.com .
The device type ID.
A unique identifier of the device that changes after every reboot. For example, the value of /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id from Linux's procfs.
The time when the device was known to have been created.
The pool of desktops or virtual machines to which the endpoint belongs.
The device hostname.
The Virtual LAN identifier.
The unique identifier of a virtual subnet.
The most recent discovery time of the device.
The unique identifier of a VM instance.
The name of the hypervisor running on the device. For example, Xen , VMware , Hyper-V , VirtualBox , etc.
The alternate device name, ordinarily as assigned by an administrator. Note: The Name could be any other string that helps to identify the device, such as a phone number; for example 310-555-1234 .
The Media Access Control (MAC) address of the endpoint.
The event occurred on a managed device.
The Integrated Circuit Card Identification of a mobile device. Typically it is a unique 18 to 22 digit number that identifies a SIM card.
The unique identifier of the network interface.
The Mobile Equipment Identifier. It's a unique number that identifies a Code Division Multiple Access (CDMA) mobile device.
The risk score as reported by the event source.
Organization and org unit related to the device.
The description of the device, ordinarily as reported by the operating system.
The most recent discovery time of the device.
The uid attribute in numeric form where applicable. Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.
The normalized risk level id.
The vendor for the device. For example Dell or Lenovo .
An alternate unique identifier of the device if any. For example the ActiveDirectory DN.
The name of the network interface (e.g. eth2).

Indicates whether the device or resource has a backup enabled, such as an automated snapshot or a cloud backup. For example, this is indicated by the cloudBackupEnabled value within JAMF Pro mobile devices or the registration of an AWS ARN with the AWS Backup service.
The peripheral devices that are attached or connected to the device.
The region where the virtual machine is located. For example, an AWS Region.

The operating system assigned Machine ID. In Windows, this is the value stored at the registry path: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Cryptography\MachineGuid . In Linux, this is stored in the file: /etc/machine-id .
If running under a process namespace (such as in a container), the process identifier within that process namespace.
The vendor or manufacturer of the endpoint's network interface controller (NIC), as identified from the MAC address.
The unique identifier of the cloud autoscale configuration.
An Embedded Identity Document, is a unique serial number that identifies an eSIM-enabled device.
The event occurred on a personal device.
The geographical location of the device.
The time when the device was known to have been created.

The physical or virtual network interfaces that are associated with the device, one for each unique MAC address/IP address/hostname/name combination. Note: The first element of the array is the network information that pertains to the event.

The Apple assigned Unique Device Identifier (UDID). For iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, watchOS and visionOS devices, this is the UDID. For macOS devices, it is the Provisioning UDID. For example: 00008020-008D4548007B4F26
The unique identifier of the device. For example the Windows TargetSID or AWS EC2 ARN.
The event occurred on a trusted device.
The endpoint hardware information.
The time when the device was last known to have been modified.
The information describing an instance of a container. A container is a prepackaged, portable system image that runs isolated on an existing system using a container runtime like containerd.
The unique identifier of the Virtual Private Cloud (VPC).
The device IP address, in either IPv4 or IPv6 format.
The subnet mask.
The time the system was booted.
A list of agent objects associated with a device, endpoint, or resource.
The initial discovery time of the device.
The model of the device. For example ThinkPad X1 Carbon .
Describes the risk associated with the finding.

The name or identifier of the message context. In AI systems, this could be the conversation ID, session name, thread identifier, or interaction name (e.g., 'user-session-123', 'conversation-abc', 'chat-thread-456').

The server or service handling the request. In AI systems, this represents the AI service, API endpoint, or agent that processes and responds to requests (e.g., OpenAI API service, Claude API service, internal AI model service).

The initiating client application. In AI systems, this represents the client-side application or framework that initiates requests (e.g., LangChain application, web browser, mobile app, SDK implementation).
The unique identifier of the message context. This could be a session ID, conversation ID, or other unique identifier that allows correlation of messages within the same context.
The normalized caption of the ai_role_id .
Specifies the functional role of the AI within the context of this message, such as retrieving information, assisting reasoning, executing a tool, or generating content.
Number of tokens in the model's response/completion for this message.
The text of the input prompt provided to the model for this message. This is the verbatim instruction, query, or context supplied to the AI system that drove the operation.
Number of tokens in the input prompt for this message.
The text of the model's response generated for this message. For agent-mediated operations, this is the content returned by the assistant, tool, or agent.
Total number of tokens used for this message (prompt + completion).
The uid attribute in numeric form where applicable. Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.
The permissions mask that was requested by the process.
The risk score as reported by the event source.
The specific type of Launch activity, normalized to the caption of the launch_type_id value. In the case of Other it is defined by the event source.
Authorization Result/outcome, e.g. allowed, denied.
Details about the Identity/Access management policies that are applicable.

Indicates that the event is considered to be an alertable signal. Should be set to true if disposition_id = Alert among other dispositions, and/or risk_level_id or severity_id of the event is elevated. Not all control events will be alertable, for example if disposition_id = Exonerated or disposition_id = Allowed .
Describes the outcome or action taken by a security control, such as access control checks, malware detections or various types of policy violations.
The normalized risk level id.

The time of the most recent event in an aggregate ( count > 1). Do not populate for discrete, point-in-time events - use time alone. Subclasses such as findings may redefine this for their own time-range semantics.
The category unique identifier of the event. Each event class belongs to exactly one category. Producers and mappers must set this to the category defined by the event class being used.
The ATT&CK® or ATLAS™ Matrix version.
The Technique object describes the MITRE ATT&CK® or ATLAS™ Technique ID and/or name associated to an attack.
The Mitigation object describes the MITRE ATT&CK® or ATLAS™ Mitigation ID and/or name that is associated to an attack.
The Sub-technique object describes the MITRE ATT&CK® or ATLAS™ Sub-technique ID and/or name associated to an attack.
The Tactic object describes the Tactic ID and/or name associated to an attack.
The normalized caption of action_id .
The exit code reported by a process when it terminates. The convention is that zero indicates success and any non-zero exit code indicates that some error occurred.

The time of the earliest event in an aggregate ( count > 1). Do not populate for discrete, point-in-time events - use time alone. Subclasses such as findings may redefine this for their own time-range semantics.
The event category name, as defined by category_uid value: System Activity .
Human-readable name for the agent. For example: Q4 Analysis Agent or Model Tester Agent .
The agent framework, normalized to the caption of the type_id value.

The version of the agent: the agent's own code or configuration revision (e.g., 1.4.2 ), distinct from the version of the model backing it (carried on ai_model.version ). Enables correlation of behavioral changes with charter or configuration revisions across agent versions.

The stable logical identifier for the agent, assigned by the agent's authoritative source (e.g., its control plane, registry, or issuing identity provider). Persists across restarts and instances. Producers populate this from whatever identity they observe: for a runtime that owns the agent, this is its issued ID; for a gateway or proxy, it is typically derived from the agent's credential. Multipl

The normalized identifier for the agent framework. Different agent frameworks have different identity, tool-call, and delegation semantics, so recording the framework enables cross-framework normalization. Communication protocols (e.g., MCP, A2A) are a property of individual operations rather than the agent itself, and are surfaced on the relevant operation rather than here.

The AI model backing this agent at the time of the recorded event. An agent's model may change across instances or versions; this captures the model in use for the specific logged activity or delegation.

A document that defines an AI agent's durable role, responsibilities, constraints, and operating boundaries. When available, populate hashes on the file for content integrity and signatures for provenance. Integrity of the event that reports this agent is provided separately by the record_integrity profile.

Identifier for a specific running instance or session of the agent, distinct from the stable logical uid . An instance is a single materialization of the agent: a conversation, session, or run. It may persist across restarts (a session that is suspended and later resumed keeps the same instance_uid ) and may span multiple cooperating runtime components, so several events can share one instance_uid
The uid attribute in numeric form where applicable. Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.

The source-specific status or error code as reported by the event source. For example, a Windows logon failure code ( 0x18 ), an HTTP response code ( 403 ), or an AWS API error code. This preserves the original code for detailed troubleshooting beyond what status_id conveys.

A human-readable description of the event, as defined by the source. This should be a concise, meaningful summary suitable for display in a UI or alert notification - not a raw log line. For example: "User john_doe logged in from 10.0.0.1." rather than a raw syslog string.
Human-readable model name. For example: gpt-4o , claude-3-sonnet , or text-embedding-ada-002 .
Model version identifier. For example: 2024-05-13 , v2.1.0 , or beta .
The unique identifier of the AI model.
AI service provider or organization name. For example: OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , or Internal .
The uid attribute in numeric form where applicable. Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.

The event/finding type ID. It identifies the event's semantics and structure. Producers and mappers must compute this as class_uid * 100 + activity_id . It uniquely identifies the combination of event class and activity across the entire schema. For example, Detection Finding: Create is 200401 .

The normalized identifier of the activity that triggered the event. Each event class defines its own set of activity values. Use 0 (Unknown) when the activity cannot be determined. Use 99 (Other) when the activity does not match any defined value, in which case activity_name must be populated with the source-specific label.

Unique identifier for this delegation context. Must be stable across the lifetime of the delegation and generated by a trusted issuing authority (e.g., an OAuth authorization server, cloud STS, IAM broker, or orchestration gateway) rather than self-asserted by the delegate. All events executed under this delegation share this identifier.
The time when the delegation was issued by the issuing authority.

The unique identifier of the trusted issuing authority (e.g., an OAuth authorization server, cloud STS, IAM broker, orchestration gateway, or SDK wrapper) that generated this delegation. Enables verification that delegation IDs were issued by an authorized component rather than self-asserted by the delegate.

The delegation identifier of the parent delegation, if this delegation was created by re-delegating authority to another party (e.g., a downstream service or automated process). This creates a parent-child relationship that enables tracking the complete chain of delegation ancestry. Does not indicate that the delegate was instantiated or spawned by the parent's delegate; that relationship, if any,
The time when the delegation was issued by the issuing authority.
The disposition name, normalized to the caption of the disposition_id value. In the case of 'Other', it is defined by the event source.

The normalized identifier of the event/finding severity. The normalized severity is a measurement the effort and expense required to manage and resolve an event or incident. Smaller numerical values represent lower impact events, and larger numerical values represent higher impact events.
The time when the process was terminated.
The process integrity level, normalized to the caption of the integrity_id value. In the case of 'Other', it is defined by the event source (Windows only).
The user under which this process is running.
The full command line used to launch an application, service, process, or job. For example: ssh user@10.0.0.10 . If the command line is unavailable or missing, the empty string '' is to be used.
The time when the process was created/started.
The group under which this process is running.

An unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs that represent a process extended attribute. For example: process security context attributes, process resource limits, container-specific attributes, or platform-specific process metadata not covered by standard OCSF attributes.
The audit user assigned at login by the audit subsystem.

The parent process of this process object. It is recommended to only populate this field for the top-level process object, to prevent deep nesting. Additional ancestry information can be supplied in the ancestry attribute.
The list of loaded module names.
The friendly name of the process, for example: Notepad++ .
A unique process identifier that can be assigned deterministically by multiple system data producers.
The working directory of a process.
The uid attribute in numeric form where applicable. Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.
The Windows services that this process is hosting.
The effective group under which this process is running.
Environment variables associated with the process.

The autonomous AI agent that this process is running or hosting, if applicable. Populate when the process serves as the runtime environment for an AI agent (e.g., a Python process executing a LangChain agent or hosting an MCP server). When a process hosts multiple agents and the activity cannot be attributed to one specifically, use hosted_ai_agent_list instead.
If running under a process namespace (such as in a container), the process identifier within that process namespace.
The process file path.
The time when the process was terminated.
The time when the process was created/started.
The effective user under which this process is running.
The identifier of the process thread associated with the event, as returned by the operating system.
The name of the containment jail (i.e., sandbox). For example, hardened_ps, high_security_ps, oracle_ps, netsvcs_ps, or default_ps.

The list of autonomous AI agents hosted by this process. Use when a single process hosts multiple agents (e.g., an IDE running several coding agents within the same host process) and the producer cannot attribute a specific activity to a single agent. When attribution is available, populate the singular ai_agent attribute instead.
A unique identifier for this process assigned by the producer (tool). Facilitates correlation of a process event with other events for that process.

An array of Process Entities describing the extended parentage of this process object. Direct parent information should be expressed through the parent_process attribute. The first array element is the direct parent of this process object. Subsequent list elements go up the process parentage hierarchy. That is, the array is sorted from newest to oldest process. The information describing an instance of a container. A container is a prepackaged, portable system image that runs isolated on an existing system using a container runtime like containerd.
The user session under which this process is running.
The normalized identifier of the process integrity level (Windows only).
The process file object.
The process identifier, as reported by the operating system. Process ID (PID) is a number used by the operating system to uniquely identify an active process.

The event activity name, as defined by the activity_id . When activity_id is 99 (Other), this attribute must contain the source-specific activity label. For all other activity_id values, this must match the caption defined for that activity_id enum value.
The number of events aggregated into this single record. Only populate for aggregate events. When set, start_time and end_time should also be provided to define the aggregation window.
The elapsed time of the aggregation window in milliseconds, from start_time to end_time . Only populate for aggregate events ( count > 1). The value should equal end_time - start_time .
The event class name, as defined by class_uid value: Process Activity .

The action taken by a control or other policy-based system leading to an outcome or disposition. An unknown action may still correspond to a known disposition. Refer to disposition_id for the outcome of the action.
The confidence, normalized to the caption of the confidence_id value. In the case of 'Other', it is defined by the event source.
The identifier of the user, system, or organization that contributed the indicator.
Specifies the type of detection pattern used to identify the associated threat indicator.
A unique identifier assigned by an external system for cross-referencing.
The timestamp of the last modification or update to the indicator.
A threat actor is an individual or group that conducts malicious cyber activities, often with financial, political, or ideological motives.
Tags or keywords associated with the indicator to enhance searchability.
Any pertinent script information related to an indicator or OSINT analysis.
The expiration date of the indicator, after which it is no longer considered reliable.
The specific detection pattern or signature associated with the indicator.
The OSINT indicator type.
The timestamp indicating when the associated indicator or intelligence was added to the system or repository.
Lockheed Martin Kill Chain Phases pertinent to an indicator or OSINT analysis.
Any pertinent autonomous system information related to an indicator or OSINT analysis.
A list of Malware objects, describing details about the identified malware.
The OSINT indicator type ID.
The timestamp when the indicator was initially created or identified.
Any email information pertinent to an indicator or OSINT analysis.
Any analytics related to an indicator or OSINT analysis.
Any pertinent WHOIS information related to an indicator or OSINT analysis.

The Traffic Light Protocol (TLP) was created to facilitate greater sharing of potentially sensitive information and more effective collaboration. TLP provides a simple and intuitive schema for indicating with whom potentially sensitive information can be shared.

A grouping of adversarial behaviors and resources believed to be associated with specific threat actors or campaigns. Intrusion sets often encompass multiple campaigns and are used to organize related activities under a common label.
The expiration date of the indicator, after which it is no longer considered reliable.
The name is a pointer/reference to an attribute within the OCSF event data. For example: file.name.

MITRE ATT&CK Tactics, Techniques, and/or Procedures (TTPs) pertinent to an indicator or OSINT analysis.

Any digital signatures or hashes related to an indicator or OSINT analysis.

The campaign object describes details about the campaign that was the source of the activity.
The actual indicator value in scope, e.g., a SHA-256 hash hexdigest or a domain name.
Analyst commentary or source commentary about an indicator or OSINT analysis.
Any pertinent subdomain information - such as those generated by a Domain Generation Algorithm - related to an indicator or OSINT analysis.
The timestamp indicating when the associated indicator or intelligence was added to the system or repository.
Any pertinent geolocation information related to an indicator or OSINT analysis.

Related reputational analysis from third-party engines and analysts for a given indicator or OSINT analysis.
The normalized severity level of the threat indicator, typically reflecting its potential impact or damage.
The unique identifier for the OSINT object.
The confidence of an indicator or analysis, normalized to the caption of the confidence_id value. In the case of 'Other', it is defined by the event source or analyst.

The normalized identifier of the confidence level, reflecting the accuracy or pertinence of the OSINT indicator or analysis. A low confidence indicates that the collected information lacked sufficient detail or accuracy to fully qualify the indicator as malicious. When the value is 99 (Other), the confidence attribute must contain the source-specific label.
The source URL of an indicator or OSINT analysis, e.g., a URL back to a TIP, report, or otherwise.
The timestamp of the last modification or update to the indicator.

Provides a reference to an external source of information related to the CTI being represented. This may include a URL, a document, or some other type of reference that provides additional context or information about the CTI.
A CIDR or network block related to an indicator or OSINT analysis.
Any pertinent file information related to an indicator or OSINT analysis.
Represents the severity level of the threat indicator, typically reflecting its potential impact or damage.
The detection pattern type, normalized to the caption of the detection_pattern_type_id value. In the case of 'Other', it is defined by the event source.

Unique identifier of this attestation. It distinguishes an individual attestation, such as a single entry within a tamper-evident chain, from the chain as a whole. See chain_uid for the identifier of the chain itself.

One or more digital signatures, each computed over this event's fingerprint and thereby over the event's canonical serialization, each bound to a verifiable identity. The first entry is typically the producer; additional entries carry co-signatures such as a notary or witness over the same event. The signing algorithm, certificate or public-key material, and signing time are carried within each di

The fingerprint of this event's canonical serialization. If signatures are present, each signature is computed over this fingerprint. Without signatures, the fingerprint alone still detects accidental alteration or corruption of the event. The next event in a chain references this value through its own prev_event.fingerprint .

Unique identifier of the authority that produced this attestation. When the attestation has a signature, authority_uid ties the signing credential to a known party: because signing credentials rotate and expire, a verifier uses this identifier to confirm that the credential belongs to the expected authority, rather than to a different holder of some otherwise-valid credential. Where multiple signa

Identifier of the append-only chain, such as a forensic or audit log, that this event belongs to. It groups a sequence of attestations so that an independent verifier can locate and validate them in order; it identifies the chain itself and is not a reference to any event outside of this one. Stable for the lifetime of the chain. For example, every attestation produced during a single agent sessio
Reference to the previous event in a tamper-evident chain, carrying that event's fingerprint together with locator attributes for retrieval. Absent on the first, or genesis, event of a chain.
The fingerprint value. Note: This uses type file_hash_t ("Hash"), which has been generalized for all fingerprints but retains the same name and caption for backwards compatibility.
The encoding of the value attribute, normalized to the caption of encoding_id . In the case of Other , it is defined by the event source.
The algorithm or scheme used to create the fingerprint, normalized to the caption of algorithm_id . In the case of Other , it is defined by the event source.
The identifier of the normalized algorithm or scheme, which was used to create the fingerprint.
The normalized identifier of the encoding used to represent the fingerprint bytes as the string in value . A verifier must decode value using this encoding to recover the raw hash bytes.

The canonical serialization scheme used to produce the deterministic byte sequence that was fingerprinted, normalized to the caption of serialization_id . In the case of Other , it is defined by the event source.

The identifier of the normalized canonical serialization scheme used to produce the deterministic byte sequence that was fingerprinted. A verifier must apply the same scheme to reproduce the fingerprinted input. The normalized confidence refers to the accuracy of the security control or alert. An analytic with a low confidence means that the alerts may be noisy or may not be malicious in nature.

The Organization object containing details about the organizational unit or management structure that governs the account, subscription, or project where the event or finding was created. This object includes properties such as the organization name, unique identifier, type, and other organizational metadata. The unique name of the Cloud services provider where the event or finding was created. Examples include AWS, Azure, GCP (Google Cloud Platform), Oracle Cloud, IBM Cloud, Alibaba Cloud, or other public, private, or hybrid cloud providers.

The cloud region where the event or finding was created, as defined by the cloud provider. The process that initiated the activity.
The user session from which the activity was initiated.
The user that initiated the activity or the user context from which the activity was initiated.
The client application or service that initiated the activity. This can be in conjunction with the user if present. Note that application is distinct from the process if present.
Provides details about an authorization, such as authorization outcome, and any associated policies related to the activity/event.
The actor's role, or as an alternative to user or process when the role is serving as a security principal for the operation that initiated the activity.
This object describes details about the Identity Provider used.

The normalized status of the event outcome. Use this family of attributes to convey the outcome of the activity described by the event. Producers should map their source outcome to 1 (Success) or 2 (Failure). Use 0 (Unknown) when the outcome cannot be determined, and 99 (Other) with a populated status string when the source value does not map cleanly.
The name of the rule that generated the event.
The rule type.
The rule version. For example: 1.1 .
The description of the rule that generated the event.
The unique identifier of the rule that generated the event.
The rule category.
The rule response time duration, usually used for challenge completion time.
The rule trigger condition for the rule. For example: SQL_INJECTION.
The data in a request that rule matched. For example: '["10","and","1"]'.
The location of the matched data in the source which resulted in the triggered firewall rule. For example: HEADER.
The rate limit for a rate-based rule.
The sensitivity of the firewall rule in the matched event. For example: HIGH.
The uid attribute in numeric form where applicable. Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.
The size of the original event data (as captured in raw_data ) in bytes, before OCSF normalization. Useful for metering and capacity planning.

The event status label, normalized to the caption of the status_id value. When status_id is 99 (Other), this attribute must contain the source-specific status label. For all other values, this must match the caption defined for that status_id enum value (e.g., "Success" for status_id: 1 ).
The event/finding type name, combining the class and activity (e.g., "Detection Finding: Create" ). The value must match the class_name and activity_name joined by ": " .

The number of minutes that the reported event time is ahead or behind UTC, in the range -1,080 to +1,080. This allows consumers to reconstruct the local time at the event source. For example, US Eastern Standard Time is -300 . Populate this when the source provides local time zone information.

The event/finding severity label, normalized to the caption of the severity_id value. When severity_id is 99 (Other), this attribute must contain the source-specific severity label. For all other values, this should match the caption defined for that severity_id enum value (e.g., "High" for severity_id: 4 ).

A human-readable description providing additional context about the event outcome. Use this to convey details that go beyond the normalized status_id and source-specific status_code , such as a failure reason or error message. For example: "Account locked after 5 failed attempts." .

The primary timestamp of the event - when the activity actually occurred at the source. The time of the earliest event in an aggregate ( count > 1). Do not populate for discrete, point-in-time events - use time alone. Subclasses such as findings may redefine this for their own time-range semantics.

The full name of the observable attribute. The name is a pointer/reference to an attribute within the OCSF event data. For example: file.name . Array attributes may be represented in one of three ways. For example: resources.uid , resources[].uid , resources[0].uid .
The observable value type name.

The value associated with the observable attribute. The meaning of the value depends on the observable type. If the name refers to a scalar attribute, then the value is the value of the attribute. If the name refers to an object attribute, then the value is not populated.

The OCSF event type UID ( type_uid ) of the source event that this observable was extracted from. This field enables filtering and categorizing observables by their originating event type. For example: 300101 for Network Activity (class_uid 3001) with activity_id 1.
The observable value type identifier.

The unique identifier ( metadata.uid ) of the source OCSF event from which this observable was extracted. This field enables linking observables back to their originating event data when observables are stored in a separate location or system.
Contains the original and normalized reputation scores.

The unique identifier of a class. A class describes the attributes available in an event. Producers and mappers must set this to the uid defined in the event class definition. For example, Detection Finding is 2004 .

The time of the most recent event in an aggregate ( count > 1). Do not populate for discrete, point-in-time events - use time alone. Subclasses such as findings may redefine this for their own time-range semantics.

The primary timestamp of the event - when the activity actually occurred at the source. The confidence score as reported by the event source. If confidence_id is 99 'Other', it should be the same as confidence if both are populated.
The time when the event was transmitted from the logging device to it's next destination.
The original size of the OCSF event data in kilobytes before any truncation occurred. This field is typically populated when is_truncated is true to indicate the full size of the original event.
The log system or component where the data originated. For example, a file path, syslog server name or a Windows hostname and logging subsystem such as Security.
The time when the event was last modified or enriched.

The level at which an event was logged. This can be log provider specific. For example the audit level.
The unique tenant identifier.
The schema extensions used to create the event.

The source of the event or finding. This can be any distinguishing name for the logical origin of the data — for example, 'CloudTrail Events', or a use case like 'Attack Simulations' or 'Vulnerability Scans'.
The type of the event or finding as a subset of the source of the event. This can be any distinguishing characteristic of the data. For example 'Management Events' or 'Device Penetration Test'.
The list of profiles used to create the event. Profiles should be referenced by their name attribute for core profiles, or extension/name for profiles from extensions.

The ultimate logged time in the event pipeline - when the event reached its final destination (e.g., SIEM, data lake). If loggers is populated, this should match the logged_time of the last entry in the loggers array. This is distinct from time (when the activity occurred) and processed_time (when an intermediate system processed the event).
The event log name, typically for the consumer of the event. For example, the storage bucket name, SIEM repository index name, etc.
Sequence number of the event. The sequence number is a value available in some events, to make the exact ordering of events unambiguous, regardless of the event time precision.

An ordered array of Logger objects describing each hop in the event pipeline between the source and its final destination. Each entry captures the logging product, device, and timestamps ( logged_time , transmit_time ) at that stage. The last entry's logged_time should match metadata.logged_time .
The identifier of the original event. For example the numerical Windows Event Code or Cisco syslog code.
The entity from which the event or finding was first reported.

The time when the event was processed by an intermediate system (e.g., ETL pipeline, event processor) before reaching its final destination. Can be used with logged_time to calculate queuing duration via total_queued_duration .
The product that reported the event.

A unique identifier used to correlate this OCSF event with other related OCSF events, distinct from the event's uid value. This enables linking multiple OCSF events that are part of the same activity, transaction, or security incident across different systems or time periods.

The ultimate logged time in the event pipeline - when the event reached its final destination (e.g., SIEM, data lake). If loggers is populated, this should match the logged_time of the last entry in the loggers array. This is distinct from time (when the activity occurred) and processed_time (when an intermediate system processed the event).
The list of tags; {key:value} pairs associated to the event.
The format of data in the log where the data originated. For example CSV, XML, Windows Multiline, JSON, syslog or Cisco Log Schema.
A list of Data Classification objects, that include information about data classification levels and data category types, identified by a classifier.
The version of the OCSF schema, using Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer). For example: 1.0.0 . Event consumers use the version to determine the available event attributes.
The logging provider or logging service that logged the event. For example AWS CloudWatch or Splunk.

The amount of time an event spent in a queue awaiting processing. In this case, the value is the difference between processed_time and logged_time . This duration is inclusive of all queues between the originator of the event and the intended long-term storage destination of the event.
Debug information about non-fatal issues with this OCSF event. Each issue is a line in this string array.

The original event time as reported by the event source, preserved as a pass-through string in its native format (e.g., Syslog timestamp, Windows event time). This is not normalized to timestamp_t - the normalized equivalent is the base event time attribute. Omit if the event is generated rather than collected via logs.

The unique identifier assigned to the event in its original logging system before transformation to OCSF format. This field preserves the source system's native event identifier, enabling traceability back to the raw log entry. For example, a Windows Event Record ID, a syslog message ID, a Splunk _cd value, or a database transaction log sequence number.

The time when the event was processed by an intermediate system (e.g., ETL pipeline, event processor) before reaching its final destination. Can be used with logged_time to calculate queuing duration via total_queued_duration .
A unique identifier assigned to the OCSF event. This ID is specific to the OCSF event itself and is distinct from the original event identifier in the source system (see original_event_uid ).
The time when the event was last modified or enriched.
The time when the event was transmitted from the logging device to it's next destination.
The event log schema version of the original event. For example the syslog version or the Cisco Log Schema version
An array of transformation info that describes the mappings or transforms applied to the data.
Indicates whether the OCSF event data has been truncated due to size limitations. When true , some event data may have been omitted to fit within system constraints.

The original event/finding data as received from the source, before normalization into OCSF. Populate this with the verbatim log line, JSON payload, or other native format for forensic and debugging purposes. This field is not intended for structured querying - use the normalized OCSF attributes instead.
The administrator-supplied or application-generated name of the scan. For example: "Home office weekly user database scan", "Scan folders for viruses", "Full system virus scan"
The total size in bytes of all files that were scanned.
The type of scan.
The application-defined unique identifier assigned to an instance of a scan.
The timestamp indicating when the scan job began execution.
The type id of the scan.
The timestamp indicating when the scan job completed execution.
The timestamp indicating when the scan job began execution.
The timestamp indicating when the scan job completed execution.
The total number of files analyzed during the scan.

The total number of storage volumes examined during the malware scan.

The number of unique malware detected across all infected files.

The user under which this process is running.
The full command line used to launch an application, service, process, or job. For example: ssh user@10.0.0.10 . If the command line is unavailable or missing, the empty string '' is to be used.
The time when the process was created/started.
The group under which this process is running.

An unordered collection of zero or more name/value pairs that represent a process extended attribute. For example: process security context attributes, process resource limits, container-specific attributes, or platform-specific process metadata not covered by standard OCSF attributes.
The audit user assigned at login by the audit subsystem.

The parent process of this process object. It is recommended to only populate this field for the top-level process object, to prevent deep nesting. Additional ancestry information can be supplied in the ancestry attribute.
The list of loaded module names.
The friendly name of the process, for example: Notepad++ .
A unique process identifier that can be assigned deterministically by multiple system data producers.
The working directory of a process.

The Windows services that this process is hosting.
The effective group under which this process is running.

Communication protocols (e.g., MCP, A2A) are a property of individual operations rather than the agent itself, and are surfaced on the relevant operation rather than here.

The AI model backing this agent at the time of the recorded event. An agent's model may change across instances or versions; this captures the model in use for the specific logged activity or delegation.

A document that defines an AI agent's durable role, responsibilities, constraints, and operating boundaries. Identifier for a specific running instance or session of the agent, distinct from the stable logical uid . An instance is a single materialization of the agent: a conversation, session, or run. The identifier of the original event. For example the numerical Windows Event Code or Cisco syslog code.
The entity from which the event or finding was first reported.

The time when the event was processed by an intermediate system (e.g., ETL pipeline, event processor) before reaching its final destination. Can be used with logged_time to calculate queuing duration via total_queued_duration .
The product that reported the event.

A unique identifier used to correlate this OCSF event with other related OCSF events, distinct from the event's uid value. This enables linking multiple OCSF events that are part of the same activity, transaction, or security incident across different systems or time periods.

The ultimate logged time in the event pipeline - when the event reached its final destination (e.g., SIEM, data lake). The amount of time an event spent in a queue awaiting processing. In this case, the value is the difference between processed_time and logged_time . This duration is inclusive of all queues between the originator of the event and the intended long-term storage destination of the event.

An ordered array of Logger objects describing each hop in the event pipeline between the source and its final destination. Each entry captures the logging product, device, and timestamps ( logged_time , transmit_time ) at that stage. The last entry's logged_time should match metadata.logged_time .
The identifier of the original event. For example the numerical Windows Event Code or Cisco syslog code.
The entity from which the event or finding was first reported.

The time when the event was processed by an intermediate system (e.g., ETL pipeline, event processor) before reaching its final destination. Can be used with logged_time to calculate queuing duration via total_queued_duration .
The product that reported the event.

A unique identifier used to correlate this OCSF event with other related OCSF events, distinct from the event's uid value. This enables linking multiple OCSF events that are part of the same activity, transaction, or security incident across different systems or time periods.

The ultimate logged time in the event pipeline - when the event reached its final destination (e.g., SIEM, data lake). The logging provider or logging service that logged the event. For example AWS CloudWatch or Splunk.

The amount of time an event spent in a queue awaiting processing. In this case, the value is the difference between processed_time and logged_time . This duration is inclusive of all queues between the originator of the event and the intended long-term storage destination of the event.

Represents the severity level of the threat indicator, typically reflecting its potential impact or damage.

Unique identifier of this attestation. It distinguishes an individual attestation, such as a single entry within a tamper-evident chain, from the chain as a whole. See chain_uid for the identifier of the chain itself.

One or more digital signatures, each computed over this event's fingerprint and thereby over the event's canonical serialization, each bound to a verifiable identity. The first entry is typically the producer; additional entries carry co-signatures such as a notary or witness over the same event. The fingerprint of this event's canonical serialization. If signatures are present, each signature is computed over this fingerprint. Without signatures, the fingerprint alone still detects accidental alteration or corruption of the event. The next event in a chain references this value through its own prev_event.fingerprint .

Unique identifier of the authority that produced this attestation. When the attestation has a signature, authority_uid ties the signing credential to a known party: because signing credentials rotate and expire, a verifier uses this identifier to confirm that the credential belongs to the expected authority, rather than to a different holder of some otherwise-valid credential. Identifier of the append-only chain, such as a forensic or audit log, that this event belongs to. It groups a sequence of attestations so that an independent verifier can locate and validate them in order; it identifies the chain itself and is not a reference to any event outside of this one. Reference to the previous event in a tamper-evident chain, carrying that event's fingerprint together with locator attributes for retrieval. Absent on the first, or genesis, event of a chain.
The fingerprint value. Note: This uses type file_hash_t ("Hash"), which has been generalized for all fingerprints but retains the same name and caption for backwards compatibility.
The encoding of the value attribute, normalized to the caption of encoding_id . In the case of Other , it is defined by the event source.
The algorithm or scheme used to create the fingerprint, normalized to the caption of algorithm_id . In the case of Other , it is defined by the event source.
The identifier of the normalized algorithm or scheme, which was used to create the fingerprint.
The normalized identifier of the encoding used to represent the fingerprint bytes as the string in value . A verifier must decode value using this encoding to recover the raw hash bytes.

The canonical serialization scheme used to produce the deterministic byte sequence that was fingerprinted, normalized to the caption of serialization_id . In the case of Other , it is defined by the event source.

The identifier of the normalized canonical serialization scheme used to produce the deterministic byte sequence that was fingerprinted. The normalized status of the event outcome. Use this family of attributes to convey the outcome of the activity described by the event. Producers should map their source outcome to 1 (Success) or 2 (Failure). Use 0 (Unknown) when the outcome cannot be determined, and 99 (Other) with a populated status string when the source value does not map cleanly.

The event status label, normalized to the caption of the status_id value. When status_id is 99 (Other), this attribute must contain the source-specific status label. For all other values, this must match the caption defined for that status_id enum value (e.g., "Success" for status_id: 1 ).
The event/finding type name, combining the class and activity (e.g., "Detection Finding: Create" ). The value must match the class_name and activity_name joined by ": " .

The number of minutes that the reported event time is ahead or behind UTC, in the range -1,080 to +1,080. This allows consumers to reconstruct the local time at the event source. For example, US Eastern Standard Time is -300 . Populate this when the source provides local time zone information.

The event/finding severity label, normalized to the caption of the severity_id value. When severity_id is 99 (Other), this attribute must contain the source-specific severity label. A human-readable description providing additional context about the event outcome. Use this to convey details that go beyond the normalized status_id and source-specific status_code , such as a failure reason or error message. For example: "Account locked after 5 failed attempts." .

The observable value type identifier.

The ultimate logged time in the event pipeline - when the event reached its final destination (e.g., SIEM, data lake). The event log name, typically for the consumer of the event. For example, the storage bucket name, SIEM repository index name, etc.
Sequence number of the event. The sequence number is a value available in some events, to make the exact ordering of events unambiguous, regardless of the event time precision.

An ordered array of Logger objects describing each hop in the event pipeline between the source and its final destination. Each entry captures the logging product, device, and timestamps ( logged_time , transmit_time ) at that stage. The last entry's logged_time should match metadata.logged_time .
The identifier of the original event. For example the numerical Windows Event Code or Cisco syslog code.
The entity from which the event or finding was first reported.

The time when the event was processed by an intermediate system (e.g., ETL pipeline, event processor) before reaching its final destination. Can be used with logged_time to calculate queuing duration via total_queued_duration .
The product that reported the event.

A unique identifier used to correlate this OCSF event with other related OCSF events, distinct from the event's uid value. This enables linking multiple OCSF events that are part of the same activity, transaction, or security incident across different systems or time periods.

The ultimate logged time in the event pipeline - when the event reached its final destination (e.g., SIEM, data lake). If loggers is populated, this should match the logged_time of the last entry in the loggers array. This is distinct from time (when the activity occurred) and processed_time (when an intermediate system processed the event).
The list of tags; {key:value} pairs associated to the event.
The format of data in the log where the data originated. For example CSV, XML, Windows Multiline, JSON, syslog or Cisco Log Schema.
A list of Data Classification objects, that include information about data classification levels and data category types, identified by a classifier.
The version of the OCSF schema, using Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer). For example: 1.0.0 . Event consumers use the version to determine the available event attributes.
The logging provider or logging service that logged the event. For example AWS CloudWatch or Splunk.

The amount of time an event spent in a queue awaiting processing. In this case, the value is the difference between processed_time and logged_time . This duration is inclusive of all queues between the originator of the event and the intended long-term storage destination of the event.
Debug information about non-fatal issues with this OCSF event. Each issue is a line in this string array.

The original event time as reported by the event source, preserved as a pass-through string in its native format (e.g., Syslog timestamp, Windows event time). This is not normalized to timestamp_t - the normalized equivalent is the base event time attribute. Omit if the event is generated rather than collected via logs.

The unique identifier assigned to the event in its original logging system before transformation to OCSF format. This field preserves the source system's native event identifier, enabling traceability back to the raw log entry. For example, a Windows Event Record ID, a syslog message ID, a Splunk _cd value, or a database transaction log sequence number.

The time when the event was processed by an intermediate system (e.g., ETL pipeline, event processor) before reaching its final destination. Can be used with logged_time to calculate queuing duration via total_queued_duration .
A unique identifier assigned to the OCSF event. This ID is specific to the OCSF event itself and is distinct from the original event identifier in the source system (see original_event_uid ).
The time when the event was last modified or enriched.
The time when the event was transmitted from the logging device to it's next destination.
The event log schema version of the original event. For example the syslog version or the Cisco Log Schema version
An array of transformation info that describes the mappings or transforms applied to the data.
Indicates whether the OCSF event data has been truncated due to size limitations. When true , some event data may have been omitted to fit within system constraints.

The original event/finding data as received from the source, before normalization into OCSF. Populate this with the verbatim log line, JSON payload, or other native format for forensic and debugging purposes. The version of the agent: the agent's own code or configuration revision (e.g., 1.4.2 ), distinct from the version of the model backing it (carried on ai_model.version ). Enables correlation of behavioral changes with charter or configuration revisions across agent versions.

The stable logical identifier for the agent, assigned by the agent's authoritative source (e.g., its control plane, registry, or issuing identity provider). Persists across restarts and instances. Producers populate this from whatever identity they observe: for a runtime that owns the agent, this is its issued ID; for a gateway or proxy, it is typically derived from the agent's credential. The normalized identifier for the agent framework. Different agent frameworks have different identity, tool-call, and delegation semantics, so recording the framework enables cross-framework normalization. Communication protocols (e.g., MCP, A2A) are a property of individual operations rather than the agent itself, and are surfaced on the relevant operation rather than here.

The AI model backing this agent at the time of the recorded event. An agent's model may change across instances or versions; this captures the model in use for the specific logged activity or delegation.

A document that defines an AI agent's durable role, responsibilities, constraints, and operating boundaries. When available, populate hashes on the file for content integrity and signatures for provenance. Integrity of the event that reports this agent is provided separately by the record_integrity profile.

Identifier for a specific running instance or session of the agent, distinct from the stable logical uid . An instance is a single materialization of the agent: a conversation, session, or run. It may persist across restarts (a session that is suspended and later resumed keeps the same instance_uid ) and may span multiple cooperating runtime components, so several events can share one instance_uid
The uid attribute in numeric form where applicable. Note: Producers may populate uid_numeric only in addition to uid and not as an alternative to it.

The source-specific status or error code as reported by the event source. For example, a Windows logon failure code ( 0x18 ), an HTTP response code ( 403 ), or an AWS API error code. This preserves the original code for detailed troubleshooting beyond what status_id conveys.

A human-readable description of the event, as defined by the source. This should be a concise, meaningful summary suitable for display in a UI or alert notification - not a raw log line. For example: "User john_doe logged in from 10.0.0.1." rather than a raw syslog string.
Human-readable model name. For example: gpt-4o , claude-3-sonnet , or text-embedding-ada-002 .

The event/finding type ID. It identifies the event's semantics and structure. Producers and mappers must compute this as class_uid * 100 + activity_id . It uniquely identifies the combination of event class and activity across the entire schema. For example, Detection Finding: Create is 200401 .

The normalized identifier of the activity that triggered the event. Each event class defines its own set of activity values. Use 0 (Unknown) when the activity cannot be determined. Unique identifier for this delegation context. All events executed under this delegation share this identifier.
The time when the delegation was issued by the issuing authority.

The unique identifier of the trusted issuing authority (e.g., an OAuth authorization server, cloud STS, IAM broker, orchestration gateway, or SDK wrapper) that generated this delegation. Enables verification that delegation IDs were issued by an authorized component rather than self-asserted by the delegate.

The delegation identifier of the parent delegation, if this delegation was created by re-delegating authority to another party (e.g., a downstream service or automated process). Unique identifier of this attestation. It distinguishes an individual attestation, such as a single entry within a tamper-evident chain, from the chain as a whole. See chain_uid for the identifier of the chain itself.

One or more digital signatures, each computed over this event's fingerprint and thereby over the event's canonical serialization, each bound to a verifiable identity. The fingerprint of this event's canonical serialization. If signatures are present, each signature is computed over this fingerprint. Without signatures, the fingerprint alone still detects accidental alteration or corruption of the event. The next event in a chain references this value through its own prev_event.fingerprint .

Unique identifier of the authority that produced this attestation. When the attestation has a signature, authority_uid ties the signing credential to a known party: because signing credentials rotate and expire, a verifier uses this identifier to confirm that the credential belongs to the expected authority, rather than to a different holder of some otherwise-valid credential. Identifier of the append-only chain, such as a forensic or audit log, that this event belongs to. It groups a sequence of attestations so that an independent verifier can locate and validate them in order; it identifies the chain itself and is not a reference to any event outside of this one. Reference to the previous event in a tamper-evident chain, carrying that event's fingerprint together with locator attributes for retrieval. Absent on the first, or genesis, event of a chain.
The fingerprint value. Note: This uses type file_hash_t ("Hash"), which has been generalized for all fingerprints but retains the same name and caption for backwards compatibility.
The encoding of the value attribute, normalized to the caption of encoding_id . In the case of Other , it is defined by the event source.
The algorithm or scheme used to create the fingerprint, normalized to the caption of algorithm_id . In the case of Other , it is defined by the event source.
The identifier of the normalized algorithm or scheme, which was used to create the fingerprint.
The normalized identifier of the encoding used to represent the fingerprint bytes as the string in value . A verifier must decode value using this encoding to recover the raw hash bytes.

The canonical serialization scheme used to produce the deterministic byte sequence that was fingerprinted, normalized to the caption of serialization_id . In the case of Other , it is defined by the event source.

The identifier of the normalized canonical serialization scheme used to produce the deterministic byte sequence that was fingerprinted. Identifier for a specific running instance or session of the agent, distinct from the stable logical uid . An instance is a single materialization of the agent: a conversation, session, or run. Unique identifier of the authority that produced this attestation. Identifier of the append-only chain, such as a forensic or audit log, that this event belongs to. The unique identifier of the message context. This could be a session ID, conversation ID, or other unique identifier that allows correlation of messages within the same context.
The normalized caption of the ai_role_id .
Specifies the functional role of the AI within the context of this message, such as retrieving information, assisting reasoning, executing a tool, or generating content.
Number of tokens in the model's response/completion for this message.
The text of the input prompt provided to the model for this message. This is the verbatim instruction, query, or context supplied to the AI system that drove the operation.
Number of tokens in the input prompt for this message.
The text of the model's response generated for this message. For agent-mediated operations, this is the content returned by the assistant, tool, or agent.
Total number of tokens used for this message (prompt + completion).

Indicates that the event is considered to be an alertable signal. Should be set to true if disposition_id = Alert among other dispositions, and/or risk_level_id or severity_id of the event is elevated. Not all control events will be alertable, for example if disposition_id = Exonerated or disposition_id = Allowed .
Describes the outcome or action taken by a security control, such as access control checks, malware detections or various types of policy violations.
The normalized risk level id.

The time of the most recent event in an aggregate ( count > 1). Do not populate for discrete, point-in-time events - use time alone. Subclasses such as findings may redefine this for their own time-range semantics.
The category unique identifier of the event. Each event class belongs to exactly one category. Producers and mappers must set this to the category defined by the event class being used.
The ATT&CK® or ATLAS™ Matrix version.
The Technique object describes the MITRE ATT&CK® or ATLAS™ Technique ID and/or name associated to an attack.
The Mitigation object describes the MITRE ATT&CK® or ATLAS™ Mitigation ID and/or name that is associated to an attack.
The Sub-technique object describes the MITRE ATT&CK® or ATLAS™ Sub-technique ID and/or name associated to an attack.
The Tactic object describes the Tactic ID and/or name associated to an attack.
The normalized caption of action_id .

The time of the earliest event in an aggregate ( count > 1). Do not populate for discrete, point-in-time events - use time alone. Subclasses such as findings may redefine this for their own time-range semantics.

Human-readable name for the agent. For example: Q4 Analysis Agent or Model Tester Agent .
The agent framework, normalized to the caption of the type_id value.

The version of the agent: the agent's own code or configuration revision (e.g., 1.4.2 ), distinct from the version of the model backing it (carried on ai_model.version ). Enables correlation of behavioral changes with charter or configuration revisions across agent versions.

The stable logical identifier for the agent, assigned by the agent's authoritative source (e.g., its control plane, registry, or issuing identity provider). Persists across restarts and instances. Producers populate this from whatever identity they observe: for a runtime that owns the agent, this is its issued ID; for a gateway or proxy, it is typically derived from the agent's credential.
